confidence_why: 7 independent first-hand descriptions agree (3 state the same rule, 3 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: A measure cannot contain less than a word, but more than one word may be contained in a measure
sweep_summary: Czech (czec1258) is in the catalog as fixed-strict initial stress, deciding source Kučera 1961 (held as Harvard page scan). Of the 12 title-hit items, three are genuinely about Czech word stress: Skarnitzl & Eriksson 2017 (held by the project, read; confirms fixed initial stress on the prosodic word, non-contrastive, with no acoustic prominence), Jakobson 1926 (newly opened via the full-view archive.org scan of Selected Writings I, pp. 614-625; presupposes fixed initial stress and refines the secondary-stress picture: 3rd/5th syllable in slow speech vs 4th in allegro, plus three speech-measure laws), and Ondráčková 1961 (STUF; not obtainable, priority high). The Elsen 1995 review of Hirschmann 1994 (German/Czech accentuation) is nominally free at De Gruyter but blocked by a bot wall (priority medium). Šimík & Wierzba 2015 (open, read) is about sentence stress only and silent on word stress; Šimík & Wierzba 2012, Sturgeon 2008, Havlík 2012, Romportl 2008, Duběda 2011, Dankovičová & Dellwo 2007 and Topolińska 1959 are phrase-level prosody, intonation, rhythm, TTS or verse studies and none was readable beyond an abstract. Nothing read contradicts the catalog's classification; the deciding source stands.

new_statements.quote: The Czech language belongs to languages with fixed stress, placed on the first syllable of the prosodic word. Its function is thus demarcative, facilitating the segmentation of the stream of speech into stress groups. Lexical stress in Czech is independent of vowel quality, length, and morphological structure of the word: in the noun posouvání ("shifting"), for instance, the first syllable will be stressed although it is a prefix, and it contains the only short vowel in the word. Monosyllabic words tend to behave like clitics, typically joined prosodically to the previous word.
new_statements.citation: Skarnitzl, Radek & Eriksson, Anders (2017). The Acoustics of Word Stress in Czech as a Function of Speaking Style. Proc. Interspeech 2017, 3221-3225. doi 10.21437/Interspeech.2017-417
new_statements.reading: Fixed, non-contrastive primary stress on the first syllable of the prosodic word (weight- and morphology-insensitive), with monosyllables cliticizing; supports the catalog's fixed-strict initial coding. The newly opened Jakobson 1926/1962 (SW I pp. 614-625) adds the secondary-stress picture (σ3/σ5 in slow speech vs σ4 in allegro for 5-syllable words; speech-measure laws), which matches the catalog's reclassify note that secondaries are optional and style-dependent rather than a strict binary alternation.

new_statements.quote: Čeština patří k jazykům s přízvukem pevným, což znamená, že je přízvuk umístěn pevný počet slabik od kraje slova; jak jsme již zmínili, v češtině se nachází na první slabice prozodického slova či mluvního taktu [...]. Přízvuk tak nemá funkci distinktivní [...], nýbrž delimitativní: přízvučná slabika značí hranici (v případě češtiny začátek) mluvního taktu [...]. Přízvuk v češtině je nezávislý na kvalitě a kvantitě samohlásky a také na morfologické struktuře slova. [...] U víceslabičných slov tedy zůstává přízvuk na první slabice, pouze s výjimkou situací, kdy jim předchází jednoslabičná předložka: jedeme ˈdo Lysé ˈnad Labem.
new_statements.translation: Czech belongs to the languages with fixed stress, which means that stress is placed a fixed number of syllables from the edge of the word; as we have already mentioned, in Czech it is on the first syllable of the prosodic word or stress group [...]. Stress thus has no distinctive function [...] but a delimitative one: the stressed syllable marks the boundary (in the case of Czech, the beginning) of the stress group [...]. Stress in Czech is independent of vowel quality and quantity and also of the morphological structure of the word. [...] In polysyllabic words, then, stress stays on the first syllable, with the sole exception of situations where they are preceded by a monosyllabic preposition: jedeme ˈdo Lysé ˈnad Labem.
new_statements.citation: Skarnitzl, Radek. 2018. Fonetická realizace slovního přízvuku u delších slov v češtině [The phonetic realization of lexical stress in longer words in Czech]. Slovo a slovesnost 79(3): 199–216.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (fixed initial: alternating stress from the left) and as the existing Skarnitzl & Eriksson 2017 statement; adds the domain (prosodic word / stress group including proclitic monosyllabic prepositions), the delimitative non-contrastive function, weight- and morphology-insensitivity, the preposition-shift and clitic exceptions, and the instrumental finding that the initial stressed syllable carries no acoustic prominence (not higher, louder or longer) in 3–6-syllable words. Nothing in it supports an alternating secondary-stress pattern; it is silent on secondary stress, consistent with the catalog's no-secondary coding.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is fixed on the first syllable of the prosodic word / stress group (mluvní takt); it is non-contrastive (delimitative, marking the beginning of the stress group) and insensitive to vowel length, vowel quality and morphology. A monosyllabic preposition forms one stress group with the following word and takes the stress. Phonetically (p. 213) the stressed vowel in ordinary speech 'is not higher, stronger or longer' – Skarnitzl's LME analysis of 3–6-syllable words in three speaking styles finds no positive prominence excursion on the stressed syllable, only a weak tendency toward a post-stress F0 rise and clear word-final vowel lengthening; native speakers nevertheless locate the stress without difficulty.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed: the text never mentions vedlejší/sekundární přízvuk; the 3–6-syllable target words are coded only as stressed (first), post-stressed (second) and unstressed (later) syllables, and the only non-initial effect found is final-syllable vowel lengthening (pp. 210–211, fig. 6–7), which the author treats as a boundary cue, not as a secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: (1) Monosyllabic prepositions take the stress of the following word (ˈdo Lysé ˈnad Labem), but per Skarnitzl (2014) the stress 'not infrequently' shifts from the preposition to the following word, especially when that word is long, is an adjective rather than a noun, and when the shift yields a more regular (rhythmic) arrangement of stress groups (p. 200). (2) Monosyllables behave as clitics because connected Czech avoids two adjacent stressed syllables: enclitics (ˈjá jsem se ˈspletl) and proclitics/předrážka (ˈzavolal, že ˈnemá ˈčas) (p. 200). (3) Informal observation that disyllabic words in spontaneous speech are 'by no means always stressed' (ˈzatím pouze ˈneformální), so such words were excluded from the study (p. 204). (4) Historical dialect note: Ondráčková (1962) analysed Doudlebsko dialect speech where speakers realized stress on the penultimate syllable (p. 202).
new_statements.identity_note: The study's own material is Common Czech (obecná čeština) from 13 speakers aged 20–32 recorded in Prague; standard/Common Czech is the variety described. The paper mentions in passing that Ondráčková (1962) studied the Doudlebsko (South Bohemian) dialect, where stress was realized on the penultimate syllable (p. 202) — a dialectal deviation from the initial-stress norm, not the variety the catalog codes.

Its function is thus demarcative, facilitating the segmentation of the stream of speech into stress groups. Lexical stress in Czech is independent of vowel quality, length, and morphological structure of the word: in the noun posouvání ("shifting"), for instance, the first syllable will be stressed although it is a prefix, and it contains the only short vowel in the word. sources.locator: p. 3221 §1 Introduction (also p. 3224 §4: 'Being a language in which stress is fixed on the first syllable of a word and is not contrastive')

sources.quote: 'Czech has stress fixed to the first syllable of a word, with the exception that a monosyllabic preposition mostly forms a single metrical unit with the following word and bears stress, e.g. moře [ˈmor̝ɛ] 'sea' vs. do moře [ˈdomor̝ɛ] 'into the sea'. As is common in fixed-stress languages ... phonetic realization of Czech stress is weak (Volín 2010: 57). Vowel duration does not function as a cue to stress.' No secondary/alternating stress mentioned.

sources.citation: Jakobson, Roman (1926). Contributions to the study of Czech accent. Slavia 4: 805-816. Read in the English version: Selected Writings I: Phonological Studies (The Hague: Mouton, 1962), pp. 614-625.
sources.quote: The older Czech descriptions of modern Czech stress dealt almost exclusively with questions of the distribution of secondary accents in words and in closely tied word groups (Vorovka, Gebauer, Vaňorný, Král, etc.). ... The first paragraph of Trávníček's study discusses the place of the secondary stress in five-syllable words. Except for compounds, this stress falls as a rule on the 3rd and/or 5th syllable, while according to Král it belongs to the fourth syllable. In other words, Trávníček consistently standardizes the slow style of Czech speech, which tends toward a trochaic distribution of the breath peaks. (pp. 614-615) ... After a syllable bearing a primary word stress there can occur, within a speech measure, only an unstressed syllable. (p. 617)
sources.locator: SW I pp. 614-615 (secondary stress), p. 617 (speech-measure laws), p. 620 n.10 and p. 622 ('Czech fixed initial stress')
sources.note: A review of Trávníček 1924 that takes fixed initial (non-phonemic) word stress as given ('the Czech fixed initial stress', p. 620 n.10; Old Czech shift of stress from noun to preceding preposition, p. 621) and concentrates on secondary stress: in 5-syllable words the secondary stress is on σ3 and/or σ5 in slow speech (Trávníček's norm) but on σ4 in allegro (Král); word units = one primary-stressed word plus accentually subordinate words; three speech-measure laws (no two stressless syllables except between two stresses the second of which is primary; the syllable after a primary stress is uns…

sources.citation: Šimík, Radek & Wierzba, Marta (2015). The role of givenness, presupposition, and prosody in Czech word order: An experimental study. Semantics and Pragmatics 8(3): 1-103.
sources.quote: The utterance is divided into three phonological phrases each of which contains two prosodic words. (Short prepositions do not count as prosodic words in Czech.) It is always the rightmost prosodic word of each phrase that receives the phrasal stress. Out of these phrasal accents it is the rightmost one which realizes the main stress of the utterance.
sources.note: Entirely about sentence/phrasal stress and givenness; the only word-level remark is that short prepositions are not independent prosodic words (consistent with proclisis of prepositions to the following noun). No statement of where word stress falls.

sources.quote: In this paper, I will show how one particular host of a popular Czech TV talk show uses prosody as a means of joking or making fun of guests, and I will also show which particular aspects of prosody he uses ...
sources.note: Conversation-analytic study of prosodic stylization in a talk show; not about word stress.
